newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala names group to oversee peace, UN arrives.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala names group to oversee peace, UN arrives.

text.p: The head of a U.N. peacekeeping mission started his tenure in Guatemala on Wednesday as the government and ex-guerrillas set up a joint commission to monitor December peace accords that ended 36 years of war.
Gen. Jose Rodriguez, the Spaniard who will lead 155 U.N. peacekeepers, flew in at the start of a three-month mission to oversee the disarmament of former guerrillas.
He said the first batch of some 10 U.N. observers would arrive by the middle of February, adding that 17 countries would send observers, including 44 from Spain.

The unarmed observers, known as "blue berets," will be stationed near eight different camps where an estimated 3,000 rebel fighters will gather late this month to begin turning in weapons under international scrutiny.
Rodriguez's arrival coincided with the establishment of a watchdog commission made up of citizens, government officials and ex-rebels of the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit, known as the URNG.

"All the actors that contributed to the successful peace negotiation and now must contribute to the success of a new phase in constructing peace are represented on this commission," Jean Arnault, the United Nations moderator during the peace talks, told a news conference.
The commission was formed as aspects of the historic peace accord signed on Dec. 29 ending Latin America's longest and last guerrilla war have begun stirring controversy.

Hundreds of military police rebelled for several days over aspects of the peace accords last week, but they surrendered on Sunday after the army threatened them with heavy artillery. The police were demanding severance pay when their unit is cut under terms of the accord.

Under the peace agreement the army will be cut by one third, which is also causing confusion. In November the army pledged to make cuts across the ranks, but this week army officials said cuts would only affect the military police and enlisted men.

"(The accords) must be understood to mean that officers as well as troops are reduced. These are things that this commission will have to look at," said Jorge Soto, formerly known as commander Pablo Monsanto, one of the URNG representatives on the commission.
